questions.questionText: The two-part scientific name of an organism is called:
questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature (two-part name) gives each species a unique scientific name consisting of genus (capitalised) and species (lowercase) names.

questions.questionText: The five kingdoms of classification are:
questions.explanation: The five-kingdom system (Whittaker) classifies all organisms into Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, and Monera based on cell type and nutrition.

questions.questionText: The correct order of taxonomic hierarchy from broad to specific is:

options.text: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Class, Order, Phylum, Family, Genus, Species
Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom, Genus, Species

questions.diagram: The hierarchical classification system goes Kingdom (broadest) → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species (most specific).

questions.questionText: Which kingdom includes organisms that are multicellular and heterotrophic?
Prokaryotes lack:
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no membrane-bound nucleus. Their DNA is in a region called the nucleoid.

questions.questionText: A species can be defined as:

options.text: A group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring

questions.explanation: A biological species is a group of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations that are reproductively isolated from other such groups.

questions.questionText: Which kingdom includes organisms that obtain nutrients by absorption?
questions.diagram: Kingdom Fungi includes saprotrophic organisms that secrete enzymes externally and absorb digested nutrients.

questions.questionText: The three domains of life are:
questions.diagram: The three-domain system (Woese) classifies all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya based on rRNA sequencing differences.

questions.questionText: Viruses are classified as neither prokaryotic nor eukaryotic because they:

options.text: Are acellular and require a host cell to reproduce

questions.explanation: Viruses are acellular particles containing DNA or RNA that can only replicate inside living host cells, placing them outside the cell-based classification system.

questions.questionText: Organisms in the genus Panthera (lion, tiger, jaguar) share the same:
questions.explanation: All three cats share the genus name Panthera (genus is always the first word in binomial nomenclature), but each has a unique species name.

questions.questionText: Which characteristic places organisms in the same order?

options.text: Share more specific characteristics than members of the same family

questions.explanation: Organisms in the same order share more specific characteristics than those grouped at the family level, reflecting closer evolutionary relationships.

questions.questionText: Bacteria differ from archaea in that bacteria:

options.text: Have membrane lipids with ester bonds

questions.explanation: Bacteria have membrane lipids with ester bonds and peptidoglycan cell walls. Archaea have ether-linked lipids and lack peptidoglycan.

questions.questionText: The scientific name for humans is Homo sapiens. The word 'Homo' represents the:
questions.explanation: In binomial nomenclature, the first word is the genus (capitalised) and the second is the species (lowercase). Homo sapiens = genus Homo, species sapiens.

questions.questionText: A dichotomous key is used to:

options.text: Identify organisms by selecting between pairs of contrasting characteristics

questions.explanation: A dichotomous key is a tool for identifying organisms by presenting a series of paired choices (either/or) of characteristics, leading to identification.

questions.questionText: The correct format for writing a scientific name is:

options.text: Homo sapiens (genus capitalised, species lower case, italicised)

questions.explanation: Scientific names are italicised (or underlined in handwriting), with genus capitalised and species lower case. Written in Latin or Latinised form.

questions.questionText: Convergent evolution produces organisms that:

options.text: Are closely related but evolved similar traits independently
Look similar but are not closely related due to similar environmental pressures

questions.explanation: Convergent evolution produces analogous structures (e.g., wings of bats and insects) where unrelated organisms evolve similar traits in similar environments.

questions.questionText: Molecular phylogeny uses which molecule to determine evolutionary relationships?
questions.explanation: Molecular phylogeny compares DNA, RNA, or protein sequences to determine evolutionary relationships between organisms based on genetic similarity.

questions.questionText: A phylogenetic tree represents:

options.text: Evolutionary history and common ancestry of organisms

questions.diagram: A phylogenetic tree (cladogram) is a branching diagram showing evolutionary relationships and common ancestry among organisms.

questions.questionText: Homologous structures are those that:

options.text: Have the same function but different evolutionary origins
Have the same evolutionary origin but may have different functions

questions.questionText: Which group contains organisms with cell walls made of chitin?
questions.explanation: Fungi have cell walls made of chitin (also found in insect exoskeletons). Plants have cellulose cell walls, and animals lack cell walls.
